transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~72 minutes | Recording id ff-20251215-argus-sharedkv-09a3
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Jamie Park (Redwood SE), Samantha Li (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (ArgusCloud - Head of Platform), Marcus Lee (ArgusCloud - SRE), Ethan Rivera (ArgusCloud - ML Engineer)

Summary: Technical deep dive on multi-tenant shared KV caching for prompt prefixes and short prompts. Focus on cache key design, namespace isolation, eviction policies, collision/poisoning mitigation, metrics to measure hit rate and correctness under variable batch sizes and quantization profiles. Discussed VPC/on-prem considerations for tenant isolation and auditability.

Topics: shared KV keying, tenant isolation, eviction strategies (LRU/LFU/hybrid), prefix normalization, prompt variants, cache warming/prefetch, telemetry and safety, VPC/on-prem network separation, KMS/HSM for cache persistence encryption

Action items (read out): see action_items metadata above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Moreno: ok, thanks everyone for hopping on, um, today we wanted to run through a practical keying strategy for shared KV caches when you're serving multiple tenants from a single pool. we'll cover hit rate tradeoffs and safety controls, and we definitely want to get your constraints up front.
[00:28] Priya Shah: thx Alex, for context we run mixed latency/throughput workloads; some tenants are high-volume chat (short prompts, 30-120 tokens) and others are long document generation. our security posture requires tenant logical isolation and audit logs, and we have SOC2 + some EU data residency needs.
[00:45] Jamie Park: great, that helps. quick Q: do you plan to use a single shared prefix cache or per-tenant namespaces on the same cluster? what's the intent for memory isolation?
[01:03] Marcus Lee: we want to avoid per-tenant GPUs because cost gets out of hand. prefer shared pools but need strong logical isolation so one noisy tenant can't pollute or evict others.
[01:20] Samantha Li: right, so common pattern we recommend is tenant-namespace + key-hash salted by tenant id. keys look like: namespace:tenantid:prompt-signature where prompt-signature is a stable digest of normalized prompt prefix. that gives fast isolation while still allowing cache to be shared on the same nodes.
[01:45] Ethan Rivera: when you say normalized prompt, do you strip user-specific tokens? we have many templated prompts with variable inserts; we want to cache the template but not the filled slots.
[02:05] Jamie Park: exactly, normalize by canonicalizing template slots and bucketizing variable-length suffixes. for example strip or replace free-text slots with tokens like <USER_TEXT> before hashing. that avoids key explosion.
[02:30] Priya Shah: is there an easy way to handle paraphrase variations where prompt wording differs but semantics are same?
[02:45] Alex Moreno: paraphrase is hard; we see 2 approaches: 1) conservative normalization + larger scope for keys (lower specificity) to increase hit rate but risk returning less-tailored completions, or 2) evaluation and learned embedding-based keying: compute a short embedding of prefix and round to centroids, use centroid id as part of key. that is more complex and adds CPU cost on the edge.
[03:20] Marcus Lee: embedding-based keying also raises safety concerns: collision semantics and how to prove determinism for audits.
[03:34] Jamie Park: yes, for compliance you need deterministic transforms or to store provenance. we recommend adding a provenance blob (small meta) that records normalization steps and versioned hashing algorithm id so you can recreate keys for audits. store that in your trace logs, not in the cache value.
[03:55] Priya Shah: what about cache poisoning? say a tenant intentionally crafts prompts to cause collisions or to evict other tenants.
[04:10] Samantha Li: primary mitigations: tenant-salted keys (so collisions across tenants require collision in salt + digest), rate-limits on cache insertion/updates, and write-through validation. also keep a tenant admission policy: new tenants start in a probationary small cache slice until they prove good behavior.
[04:35] Ethan Rivera: eviction policy? LRU tends to favor recency but can be gamed by churn, LFU favors frequency but cold-starts penalize; hybrid?
[04:50] Jamie Park: our customers often use a hybrid time-decayed LFU with an upper limit per-tenant weight. we also offer quota tokens that allow the control plane to cap insertion throughput per tenant and a soft-reservation for SLA-critical tenants.
[05:15] Marcus Lee: concretely, can Redwood's runtime enforce per-tenant eviction weights on a shared node?
[05:25] Alex Moreno: yes, the serving runtime maintains per-namespace counters and a lightweight eviction scheduler. it approximates LRU via segmented queues and factors tenant weight when selecting eviction candidates. not perfect LRU but bounded worst-case.
[05:40] Priya Shah: how does batching interact with cache hits? we run continuous batching with variable batch sizes.
[05:52] Jamie Park: key point: batching increases throughput but can hide per-request cache misses; we tag each request with pre/post cache flags so tracing can attribute latencies properly. also, when a batch contains mixed-hit/miss, runtime can split path: hit tokens served from KV, misses forwarded to model VM with warmed KV state where possible.
[06:15] Ethan Rivera: warming sounds neat. do you support prefetch/prefill of KV from recent sessions?
[06:24] Samantha Li: yes, prefilling heuristics: when a conversation reaches certain pattern thresholds we proactively materialize likely next-prefixes. but prefetch increases write amplification; we recommend bounded prefetch windows and TTLs tuned per workload.
[06:40] Priya Shah: TTL strategies — fixed vs adaptive?
[06:46] Jamie Park: adaptive TTL based on observed hit half-life works well: estimate exponential decay of hit probability and set TTL to the time where hit-probability drops below configurable threshold. simpler approach: tiered TTLs by tenant SLA class.
[07:05] Marcus Lee: telemetry — what metrics should we capture to evaluate hit-rate and fairness?
[07:12] Alex Moreno: capture per-tenant hit-rate, per-key frequency sketch (we export top-k samples), insert-to-hit latency distribution, eviction reason (age/weight/quota), and collision counters. export p50/p95/p99 for cache lookup latency as separate from model latency.
[07:30] Priya Shah: how noisy are the collision counters in practice? do false positives spike with int4 quantized embeddings?
[07:40] Jamie Park: collisions from digest hashing are orthogonal to model quantization, but embedding-based keying can be impacted by quantization if embeddings are computed on-accelerator with reduced precision. we recommend computing embedding digests on a stable CPU path or applying a per-model calibration step.
[08:05] Samantha Li: on quantization more broadly: 8-bit and int4 inference profiles change latency/throughput and sometimes KV sizes (smaller KV values if using quantized cache payload). verify quantized model behavior with your prompts because output variance may affect perceived hit correctness.
[08:30] Ethan Rivera: question about private / on-prem: if we run Redwood Private inside our VPC, do we get same keys and audit hooks?
[08:42] Alex Moreno: yes, Private deploy includes the same runtime; keying proposal and provenance traces are configurable to be logged to your SIEM. for on-prem we can enable HSM/KMS integration for encrypting cache snapshot at rest and TLS mutual auth between control plane agents.
[09:00] Marcus Lee: are there network implications for cache lookups across nodes? we worry about cross-AZ latency spikes for KV lookups.
[09:10] Jamie Park: we co-locate hot partitions with model replicas using consistent hashing with zone-awareness. for writes we use async replication; reads prefer local replica with stale tolerances you can configure. if you need strict read-after-write you can set affinity to pinned node groups at cost of reduced flexibility.
[09:35] Priya Shah: pinned nodes means loss of bin-packing; cost tradeoff. ok.
[09:42] Alex Moreno: yep — that's the cost vs latency tradeoff.
[09:48] Ethan Rivera: any built-in guardrails for noisy-tenant detection?
[09:53] Samantha Li: yes, our monitoring can detect abnormal insertion rates per tenant and auto-throttle with an alert to ops. we can also flag tenant patterns that cause high eviction churn for manual review.
[10:10] Marcus Lee: curious about storage persistence — we snapshot KV for fast restart. is snapshot encrypted using our KMS?
[10:18] Jamie Park: in Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM; in Hosted we encrypt using customer-managed keys when enabled. snapshots are incremental and we include key-version metadata.
[10:30] Priya Shah: great. one more: how do we debug mismatched completions where cached output looks stale vs live model?
[10:40] Alex Moreno: store metadata with cached values: model id + model version + quantization profile + prompt-hash + creation-timestamp + provenance id. that way you can detect mismatch and optionally force model recompute. we also include an automatic staleness score that increments if model versions differ.
[11:05] Ethan Rivera: you mentioned admission/probation earlier. can you expand?
[11:12] Jamie Park: new tenants by default get a small cache quota and a higher insertion penalty. after 7 days or X successful hit-rate thresholds we promote them. that prevents attackers from flooding cache with low-value items to push others out.
[11:32] Priya Shah: do you support tenant-level snapshots for compliance or data retention deletion requests?
[11:40] Samantha Li: yes, we can garbage collect by tenant namespace and support expunge operations, plus audit logs for deletes. note: if you snapshot and ship to long-term store, ensure you apply the same deletion semantics there.
[11:58] Marcus Lee: let's talk numbers: what hit rates do you typically see for templated chat vs open-ended generation?
[12:06] Jamie Park: templated chat with good normalization can reach 40-65% hit-rate depending on traffic skew; open-ended generation is low — single digits — unless you bin by conversational turn anchors. customers often see overall 20-30% effective token-level hit if they combine prefix + KV caching + batching.
[12:30] Priya Shah: what's the observed latency reduction for a hit?
[12:35] Alex Moreno: cache-hit token emission can be 5-20ms per token on local hot path vs model token cost which is tens to hundreds ms depending on model and quantization. end-to-end p95 improvement depends on percent tokens served from cache.
[12:50] Ethan Rivera: any gotchas with streaming and partial-hits in a response?
[12:56] Jamie Park: yes — streaming with partial-hits needs careful assembly. we tag token ranges as cached vs generated and stream with boundary markers; clients should be tolerant. mismatched termination tokens are the most common bug so we add strict canonicalization.
[13:15] Priya Shah: can we get sample dashboards to visualize per-tenant fairness?
[13:20] Alex Moreno: yes we'll share example dashboards — heatmaps of eviction churn, per-tenant hit-rate, and insertion rate.
[13:30] Marcus Lee: ok what about auditability around keying algorithm changes? we need to prove in an audit that cached outputs were derived deterministically under a given keying policy.
[13:42] Samantha Li: version everything: keying-algo:v1, normalization:v2, embedding-centroids:v3. store policy id with cache entries and keep immutable policy docs. for audits, we can replay normalization steps against stored prompt snapshots.
[13:58] Ethan Rivera: is there an official Redwood spec on this? a one-pager we can circulate with legal and infosec?
[14:04] Alex Moreno: yes — we'll send the KV keying proposal doc and the safety checklist.
[14:12] Priya Shah: awesome. one last quick thing: how do you measure cross-tenant fairness numerically?
[14:19] Jamie Park: we compute per-tenant hit-rate and also Gini coefficient on hit distribution to detect imbalance. if Gini > threshold we alert and suggest re-sharding or weight changes.
[14:35] Marcus Lee: sweet. ok let's recap next steps.
[14:40] Alex Moreno: recap: Redwood shares formal keying doc + telemetry examples; Argus runs a 24h experiment and shares results; schedule on-prem pilot review. thanks all.
[14:55] Priya Shah: thanks, this was useful.
[15:00] Meeting ended.
